analysis.one_liner: Bans the secret rebates drug manufacturers pay to pharmacy benefit managers and insurers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote; it was introduced in April 2023, referred to the Senate health committee with zero cosponsors, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, when you pay for a prescription, the price you see at the pharmacy is often inflated because the drugmaker has already promised a large, hidden rebate to the middleman company — the pharmacy benefit manager — and to your insurer that steers the drug onto their list. This bill would make those hidden payments illegal, and allow discounts only if they are given at the time of purchase, so lower prices reach people when they actually buy the drug. The bill was introduced by Senator Josh Hawley, referred to the Senate health committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: People with private or employer insurance who pay out of pocket at the pharmacy. If rebates must be given as upfront discounts instead of hidden back-end payments, the cash price people see at the counter would no longer need to cover the rebate money flowing to insurers and PBMs — so insured patients, and especially the uninsured who pay full list price, could see cheaper drug costs. Plan sponsors (employers) would also gain a clearer picture of what their drug benefit really costs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients paying out of pocket for prescriptions

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes the federal safe harbor that currently protects rebates from drug manufacturers to PBMs — including rebates paid specifically to influence which formulary tier a drug sits on — under the Social Security Act's anti-kickback provisions [S2][S3].

It directly bars group health plans and health insurers from receiving manufacturer rebates on any covered drug, and requires them to make sure their PBMs do not receive such rebates either, under the Public Health Service Act, ERISA, and the Internal Revenue Code [S3].

The bill defines 'rebate' as a discount whose terms are fixed in writing at purchase but not paid at purchase — so drugmakers would have to give discounts at the point of sale, where the patient is, rather than through back-end payments to intermediaries [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The three dominant pharmacy benefit managers and the health insurers they are often affiliated with would lose the rebate revenue stream and their central role in the drug-pricing system. Brand-name drug manufacturers would lose rebates as a lever for buying formulary placement and would face pressure to cut list prices; they might respond by raising premiums or reducing discounts elsewhere.

drawbacks.text: The rebate system, whatever its faults, does lower net prices for insurers, and insurers use that savings to offset premiums. Ending back-end rebates could push up monthly premiums even as pharmacy counter prices fall — a tradeoff an honest supporter must acknowledge.

Patients with high deductibles pay the full price before insurance kicks in; if manufacturers convert rebates to point-of-sale discounts only partly, some patients could pay more upfront than they do today.
The bill was written and introduced by a single senator with no cosponsors, and it never received a committee hearing or markup where these design questions could be tested and refined.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — stop rebates from flowing to middlemen instead of to patients at the counter — targets a real and widely criticized distortion in drug pricing. The main cost is that premiums, not just pharmacy prices, are part of what people pay, and a ban on back-end rebates shifts where the savings show up. On balance this would have been a substantial win for people who pay cash at the pharmacy, but the bill was a one-page starting point with no cosponsors and no committee scrutiny, so its details were never tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate and referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it sat until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no vote, and no cosponsors ever signed on [S1][S4][S5].

narrative.text: Senator Josh Hawley introduced S. 1217, the Ending the Prescription Drug Kickback Act of 2023, on April 19, 2023 [S1][S2].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions — the only action the bill ever received [S5].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill still in committee; any bill not passed by both chambers dies when a Congress ends [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmacy benefit managers and health insurers are better off: the hidden-rebate system that routes manufacturer payments through them stays fully intact, and brand-name drugmakers keep the rebate lever they use to win formulary placement.

for.name: Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made no further progress with it; no senator joined him as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Committee where the bill sat without a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration after its referral on April 19, 2023.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there is no record of how members would have split; the bill had a Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors of either party [S4].

industries.note: PBMs are the intermediaries that negotiate drug prices for insurers and pharmacies, and manufacturer rebates are a core part of their revenue and their power over which drugs are favored. The bill removes their legal safe harbor for taking those rebates and bars them from receiving them, so their interest ran directly against patients' interest in transparent, lower counter prices.

Insurers receive manufacturer rebates on covered drugs and use them to offset premiums, but the payments are invisible to patients at the pharmacy counter. The bill would ban plans from receiving these rebates entirely.

Manufacturers currently pay large rebates to buy favorable formulary placement while keeping list prices high. The bill removes that lever, which pressures them toward lower list prices and upfront discounts — potentially helping uninsured patients most, though they could try to offset losses elsewhere.

Independent and community pharmacies are squeezed when reimbursement is set against inflated list prices net of PBMs' rebate take. If discounts had to flow at the point of sale, pharmacy reimbursement economics could improve, though the bill does not address this directly.
